summaries.gardner: Thermo Fisher has some Rule Breaker traits (top dog in a big industry, a lasting scale advantage and a share price up 28.0% in the past year), but it is a mature consolidator rather than a pioneer of an emerging industry. Its revenue grows in single digits (organic growth of 5% in Q2 2026), so it looks more like a Rule Maker than a Rule Breaker.
summaries.buffett: Thermo Fisher has an understandable franchise with recurring consumables, high switching costs, steady profits for over a decade and free cash flow close to net income ($6,337M vs $6,704M in 2025). Against Buffett's tenets, its return on capital is modest (high single digits) because of heavy acquisition goodwill and $42,549M of debt, and at about 36 times trailing GAAP earnings there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the switching costs of reagents and instruments written into validated drug processes, and inverting shows few ways the business could fail outright. The main risks are cuts to US research funding, tariffs and China exposure, integrating frequent large deals such as Clario, and paying a full price of about 27 times forward adjusted earnings.
summaries.lynch: Thermo Fisher is a classic Lynch stalwart with a simple story (sell the picks and shovels of science and drug making) and a shrinking share count (399M diluted shares in 2020 to 371M in Q2 2026). It fails his price test: a trailing P/E of about 36 against EPS growth of roughly 10% gives a PEG well above 1, and it is widely followed on Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: Thermo Fisher fits several Fisher points: a large sales and distribution organisation (Fisher Scientific), steady new products such as Orbitrap mass spectrometers and Krios cryo-electron microscopes, and long-serving management under Marc Casper since 2009. Fisher might note that growth relies heavily on acquisitions rather than internal R&D, and that operating margins (17.4% in 2025) are below their COVID-era peak.
summaries.graham: Thermo Fisher passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and EPS growth tests (diluted EPS rose from $4.92 in 2015 to $17.74 in 2025). It fails on dividend record (dividends began only in 2012) and on price, with a P/E of about 36 and P/E times P/B of roughly 170, far above his 22.5 limit.
summaries.thiel: Thermo Fisher has strong answers on distribution, durability and scale, being the largest supplier to labs and drugmakers. It is not a monopoly built on technology ten times better than rivals: Danaher, Agilent, Merck KGaA and Waters compete closely in most categories.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would see a high-quality, cash-generative compounder with improving momentum (guidance raised in April and July 2026, Q2 revenue up 10%). On his growth-adjusted valuation lens it looks fully priced at about 27 times forward adjusted earnings for roughly 9-11% EPS growth, and it is only an indirect beneficiary of the AI platform shift.
summaries.druckenmiller: Fundamentals are improving (organic growth rose to 5% in Q2 2026, adjusted EPS guidance of $24.93-$25.33 implies 9-11% growth) and the stock has risen 28.0% in a year, which fits Druckenmiller's focus on inflection and momentum. Much of the recovery is now visible in the price, and lower interest rates and a biotech funding recovery would be the main macro tailwinds.
summaries.smith: Thermo Fisher passes Smith's 'good company' test on resilience, recurring revenue and cash conversion, but its return on capital (high single digits after acquisitions) and gross margin of 41.5% are below the levels he usually seeks. With a free-cash-flow yield of about 3% it fails 'don't overpay' at today's price.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Thermo Fisher ranks poorly: operating income of $7,746M in 2025 is under 3% of an enterprise value of about $288B, and return on tangible capital is diluted by acquisitions. It is a quality business but not a cheap one by Greenblatt's measures.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool fits partly: a good business with recurring consumables, and a long-tenured, capable CEO who reinvests through acquisitions and buybacks. The third leg, reinvestment at high returns, is weaker because returns on capital are only high single digits after large deals such as PPD and Clario.
summaries.pabrai: Thermo Fisher is a durable business with a low chance of permanent loss, but there is no Dhandho-style bargain: the stock is near its 52-week high of $694.33 after rising 28.0% in a year, and the post-COVID setback is largely priced back in.
summaries.wood: Thermo Fisher supplies tools used in multiomic sequencing and proteomics (Olink, Ion Torrent, Orbitrap) and is investing in AI for drug discovery, but it is an incumbent rather than a pure disruptive-innovation play. Its single-digit growth and mature markets fall outside ARK's focus.
summaries.ackman: Thermo Fisher meets several Ackman criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with high barriers to entry and limited commodity exposure. The balance sheet carries $42,549M of debt, and at about 27 times forward adjusted earnings the price is not at the discount to intrinsic value he usually wants.
summaries.sleep: Thermo Fisher has scale economics, but it largely keeps the gains as margin rather than passing them on to customers, which is the opposite of Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model. Its long-term position looks durable but not clearly strengthening year after year.
summaries.valentine: Thermo Fisher solves a large, painful problem (giving scientists and drugmakers reliable tools, consumables and capacity) in a huge market. As a 70-year-old consolidator it is far from the young, fast-growing companies on a big wave that Valentine looked for.
summaries.nash: Thermo Fisher fails several of Nash's instant-kill tests: debt ($42,549M) far exceeds cash ($4,064M), operating margin is 17.4% and revenue growth is below 10%. It is a large, durable business with a trustworthy earnings record, but it is not the fast-growing, cash-rich trend leader his process seeks, and a simple DCF puts its value far below the $673 share price.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed at $673.20 on October 14, 2026, up 28.0% in a year and near its 52-week high of $694.33, ahead of the S&P 500's roughly 16% gain over the same period.

g4.evidence: Marc Casper has led the company since 2009 with a strong execution record, and large institutions own most of the shares, but it has no famous visionary founder or star backer.

g6.evidence: Some commentators call it expensive at about 36 times trailing GAAP earnings, but most analysts rate it a buy, so 'overvalued' is not the common view.

simple.evidence: It sells lab instruments, reagents and consumables, drug-manufacturing capacity and clinical-research services, a business a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $4.92 in 2015 to $17.74 in 2025, but revenue fell in 2023 ($44,915M to $42,857M) after COVID-19 testing demand faded.

integrity.evidence: Communication is clear and guidance is usually met or raised, but capital allocation leans on large acquisitions and management pay is tied mainly to adjusted EPS and revenue.

b6.evidence: Deals such as Clario ($8.875B, 2026), Solventum's purification business (2025) and Olink (2024) fit its strategy, but the steady stream of acquisitions looks at times like empire-building.

roic.evidence: Net income plus after-tax interest of roughly $7.9B in 2025 on about $91B of capital (equity of $52,686M plus net debt of $38,485M at June 2026) is a return of under 9%, and it relies on substantial debt.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $6,337M in 2025 against net income of $6,704M (95%), and $2,503M in the first half of 2026.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded deals that grew revenue from $32,218M in 2020 to $44,556M in 2025, but operating income was roughly flat ($7,794M to $7,746M) over that period.

safety.evidence: At $673.20 the stock trades at about 36 times trailing GAAP EPS of $18.58 and a free-cash-flow yield of about 3%, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 27 times the midpoint of 2026 adjusted EPS guidance ($24.93-$25.33) is a full but not extreme price for a high-quality leader growing EPS around 10%.

mu5.evidence: Its diversity across about a dozen end markets, recurring consumables and validated-process lock-in leave few ways for it to fail, the main ones being excess debt or a badly priced acquisition.

reinvest.evidence: It can keep reinvesting through acquisitions and capacity, but returns on recent deals have been modest, with company-wide returns on capital below 10%.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: the largest supplier of tools and services to science and drug making, growing with biologics and research spending.

ly3.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 36 is far above expected EPS growth of about 9-11% (2026 guidance).

runway.evidence: Biologics, cell and gene therapy, proteomics and clinical-trial data (Clario) give it years of growth, but the core is a mature market growing in mid single digits.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 399M in 2020 to 371M in Q2 2026 through buybacks ($4,000M in H1 2026), but insiders have been net sellers, with no notable open-market purchases.

ly8.evidence: It is a $250B-plus company covered by most large brokers and held widely by institutions.

fi4.evidence: Its Fisher Scientific channel and global sales force reach almost every lab, making it the default one-stop supplier.

longterm.evidence: Management invests through cycles (capacity, R&D and deals) but also targets steady annual adjusted EPS growth and large buybacks.

gr1.evidence: Revenue was $44,556M in 2025 and its market value is around $250B.

ni10.evidence: Net income was positive every year from 2016 ($2,022M) to 2025 ($6,704M).

gr4.evidence: Thermo Fisher began paying a dividend only in 2012, so it lacks a 20-year record.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $4.92 in 2015 to $17.74 in 2025, an increase of about 260%.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 36 times a P/B of about 4.7 (equity of $52,686M on 371M shares) gives roughly 170, far above 22.5.

timing.evidence: Biopharma demand is recovering (organic growth reached 5% in Q2 2026), though US academic and government funding remains under pressure.
